chapter_title: Securing Incident Response with IAM and AWS Organizations

screens.title: Securing Incident Response with IAM & AWS Organizations
screens.subtitle: Design temporary, MFA-protected cross-account access and organizational guardrails so responders can act without increasing risk.

narration.text: In an incident you need speed, but speed without control becomes risk. This lesson explains how to give incident responders the elevated access they need, while keeping that access short-lived, auditable, and constrained. You will learn why dedicated IAM roles are safer than granting user permissions, how to require multi-factor authentication when roles are assumed, and how AWS Organizations Service Control Policies act as a last-resort guardrail across accounts. We will also cover temporary credentials from the Security Token Service and practical steps to design cross-account trust policies so a security team in one account can troubleshoot resources in another. For example, imagine a responder needing to run diagnostics in production: a scoped cross-account role with an MFA condition and a limited session duration gives just enough access for the task while minimizing exposure. Finally, we discuss common mistakes such as over-privileged roles, long-lived keys, and disabling logs, and how to prevent them with SCPs and careful role design. By the end of this chapter you will know how to balance practical operational access with strong security controls.

keyIdea.text: Provide temporary, MFA-protected, least-privilege cross-account access and enforce organizational guardrails with SCPs to protect forensic integrity during incidents.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: We will focus on practical, assessment-ready skills that you can apply during real incidents. First, you will implement least-privilege controls for incident roles and users so responders only receive the permissions they need and nothing extra. You will also design cross-account access patterns that let your security or primary account assume roles in target accounts with MFA enforced, which centralizes identity while keeping account-level permissions separate. Next, you will configure Service Control Policies in AWS Organizations to create hard guardrails that prevent destructive actions such as deleting audit logs, even if a responder has elevated IAM permissions. You will learn to use temporary credentials via the Security Token Service to avoid long-lived keys and to require MFA when roles are assumed. Finally, you will identify common mistakes like over-privilege and lack of audit trails and adopt mitigations such as break-glass procedures, tight logging, and regular permission reviews. Each objective maps to a competency milestone so you can verify the configuration in a lab or exam-style task.

screens.title: Principle of Least Privilege for Incident Response
screens.subtitle: Define minimal, task-specific permissions and prefer role assumption over user keys

narration.text: The principle of least privilege means assigning the minimum permissions necessary for a user or role to accomplish a task. For incident response this is critical because responders often need elevated rights temporarily; granting broad rights permanently is an unacceptable risk. Practically, implement least privilege by creating dedicated incident response roles scoped to only the actions needed for diagnostics and remediation. For example, a role used to investigate EC2 may include ec2:DescribeInstances and ssm:StartSession but not iam:CreateUser. A common misconception is that broad permissions speed response. In reality, over-privilege increases the attack surface and can enable accidental destructive actions, such as deleting logs or terminating instances. Instead, prepare multiple narrowly scoped roles for different types of tasks and document which role to assume for each scenario. Combine these scoped roles with permission boundaries and conditional checks like MFA requirement so that even if a role is compromised it cannot be used outside intended constraints. Your takeaway: planned, narrow roles plus temporary sessions let responders act quickly while keeping the environment protected. Principle of Least Privilege for Incident Response means least privilege for ir means narrow, task-specific roles that limit what responders can do and reduce blast radius.. In practical terms, define minimal, task-specific permissions and prefer role assumption over user keys. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Create Dedicated IAM Roles and Assume-Role Pattern
screens.subtitle: Centralize identity, decentralize permissions using assume-role for incident responders

narration.text: A robust pattern is to create dedicated IAM roles for incident responders in target accounts and let responders assume those roles from a central account. This centralization keeps responder identities managed in one place while permissions remain scoped to each account's resources. The flow is: responder authenticates to the primary account with MFA, the primary account grants sts:AssumeRole for a specific target role, and the target role's trust policy allows that primary account to assume it under conditions such as MFA or an ExternalId. A practical example: your security team in account A needs to inspect resources in production account B. Define CrossAccountIncidentResponder in account B with a trust policy that permits account A to assume that role only if aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true. One misconception is that the cross-account trust must include every responder; instead, trust the account or a specific role, and use the target role's permissions to limit actions. Also log assume-role events in CloudTrail to keep an audit trail. This split-of-responsibility pattern provides operational flexibility without sacrificing account-level control. Create Dedicated IAM Roles and Assume-Role Pattern means manage identities centrally and create per-account roles with scoped permissions and trust policies to enable safe cross-account access.. In practical terms, centralize identity, decentralize permissions using assume-role for incident responders. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Cross-Account Assume-Role
Process Flow

Assume-role sequence

01 Authenticate with MFA
Responder signs into the primary account and proves MFA presence.
02 Assume target role
Use sts:AssumeRole to obtain temporary credentials for the target account role.
03 Perform scoped actions
Carry out diagnostics within the permission boundaries of the assumed role.
Pro tip
Use an ExternalId in trust policies when cross-account trust is used by third parties or automation to prevent confused deputy problems.
Example
Trust relationship requires MFA and the primary account as principal.
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root" },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": { "aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true" },
        "StringEquals": { "sts:ExternalId": "YourUniqueExternalId" }
      }
    }
  ]
}
Key Takeaway

Trust policies plus MFA conditions let the primary account assume scoped roles in target accounts safely and audibly.

screens.title: Require MFA in Trust Policies
screens.subtitle: Enforce aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent so assume-role requires an MFA device

narration.text: Requiring MFA in a trust policy is a simple and highly effective control. The condition aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent must evaluate to true for an assume-role operation to succeed. This means that even if an attacker has stolen long-lived credentials or a session token, they cannot assume the privileged role unless they also control the MFA device. Implement this by adding a Bool condition to the trust policy. A frequent misconception is that MFA on the user alone is sufficient; you should explicitly require MFA at assume-time in the trust policy since roles may be assumed from different identities or automation contexts. Another useful element is ExternalId to further restrict who can assume the role. Practically, test enforcement by attempting an AssumeRole without an MFA authentication step and confirm it is denied. The protection works best combined with short STS session durations and logging of assume-role events in CloudTrail so you can monitor and alert on unusual assume attempts. Require MFA in Trust Policies means add aws:multifactorauthpresent condition to trust policies so assume-role only works when mfa is present.. In practical terms, enforce aws:multifactorauthpresent so assume-role requires an mfa device. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › MFA in Trust Policies
Definition

Require MFA at role assumption

Add a Bool condition that demands aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent equals true in the trust policy.

Trust policy example
{
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:root"},
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
      "Condition": {"Bool": {"aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent": "true"}}
    }
  ]
}
Testing checklist
  • Attempt AssumeRole without MFA and expect access denied.
  • Assume with MFA and confirm temporary credentials are issued.
  • Verify CloudTrail logs show the assume-role event and the principal used.
Common misconception
MFA on the user is not the same as requiring MFA when a role is assumed — trust policies must require it explicitly.
Key takeaway
Enforce aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent in trust policies and use short STS sessions to minimize exposure.

screens.title: Use STS Temporary Credentials and CLI Profiles
screens.subtitle: Avoid long-lived keys by assuming roles and using temporary sessions in automation and CLI

narration.text: Temporary credentials from the Security Token Service reduce the risk of key compromise because they expire automatically. During incident response, assume a role to obtain short-lived access, rather than distributing long-lived access keys. Tools like aws-vault or native CLI profiles that use role_arn and mfa_serial make this practical. A typical flow is to configure a profile that uses your primary account credentials as the source_profile and points to a cross-account role_arn to assume; the CLI will prompt for an MFA code and fetch temporary credentials for the session. A misconception is that temporary credentials remove the need for MFA — they work best together. Also avoid embedding temporary credentials in scripts; prefer profiles or environment variables managed by secure tooling that rotates and expires them. Finally, log and audit STS usage in CloudTrail so you can see who assumed which role and when, which is crucial for post-incident review and compliance. Use STS Temporary Credentials and CLI Profiles means use sts to issue time-limited credentials via role assumption; integrate mfa via mfa_serial in cli profiles or secure tooling like aws-vault.. In practical terms, avoid long-lived keys by assuming roles and using temporary sessions in automation and cli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › STS & Temporary Credentials
Definition

Temporary credentials via STS

Assume a role to obtain temporary, limited-privilege credentials that expire automatically.

CLI profile example
[profile cross-account-ir]
role_arn = arn:aws:iam:::role/CrossAccountIncidentResponder
source_profile = default
mfa_serial = arn:aws:iam:::mfa/your-mfa-device
Run the command and enter an MFA code when prompted to receive temporary credentials for the session.
Practical notes
  • Avoid long-lived access keys for responders; prefer assume-role flows.
  • Use tools like aws-vault to manage session injection and MFA prompts securely.
  • Ensure session duration is appropriately short for the task and logged.
Common mistake
Embedding temporary credentials in automation without rotation and expiry monitoring.
Key Takeaway

Temporary credentials plus MFA reduce long-lived key exposure and improve auditability of assume-role events.

screens.title: Cross-Account Trust Policies in Practice
screens.subtitle: How to structure trust and permission policies for target account roles

narration.text: Designing cross-account trust involves two pieces: a trust policy in the target account that allows the primary account to assume a role, and a permissions policy attached to the role that limits actions within the target account. The trust policy should reference the principal — typically the primary account's ARN — and enforce conditions such as aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent and possibly an ExternalId. The permissions policy should only include actions required for the responder's tasks, for example ec2:DescribeInstances, cloudwatch:GetMetricData, and ssm:StartAutomationExecution for troubleshooting. A common error is over-scoping the permissions policy or relying solely on trust conditions without auditing. Also avoid trusting individual users directly when the primary account can instead allow a known responder role to assume; this improves manageability. When building the target role, set a reasonable maximum session duration, enable CloudTrail logging for assume-role events, and avoid attaching broad policies like AdministratorAccess. By separating trust and permissions and logging every assume operation, you gain clear accountability and minimized blast radius during incidents. Cross-Account Trust Policies in Practice means trust policy controls who can assume a role and under what conditions; permissions policy determines what that assumed role can do in the target account.. In practical terms, how to structure trust and permission policies for target account roles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Define who can assume the role and under which conditions like MFA and ExternalId.

  • cloudwatch:GetMetricData
  • ssm:StartAutomationExecution

  • Log assume-role and API activity in CloudTrail and alert on unusual patterns.
  • Avoid AdministratorAccess and use permission boundaries where needed.

screens.title: SCPs vs IAM Policies — Guardrails and Permissions
screens.subtitle: How Service Control Policies differ from and complement IAM policies

narration.text: Service Control Policies and IAM policies operate at different layers and serve different purposes. IAM policies grant or deny permissions at the identity or resource level. SCPs, in contrast, set the maximum available permissions for accounts or organizational units — they are a preventative guardrail. A key consequence is that an SCP can block an action even if an IAM role explicitly allows it. For incident response this is valuable: an SCP can explicitly deny actions like deleting CloudTrail logs or disabling detection services across your production OU so that no responder or root user can remove forensic evidence. A common misconception is that SCPs replace IAM policies; they do not. Instead, use SCPs to define a safe perimeter and IAM policies to provide the day-to-day operational permissions within that perimeter. When designing SCPs, be conservative for critical OUs and test thoroughly, because SCPs apply to all principals in affected accounts including root. The combination of scoped IAM roles plus conservative SCPs creates a layered defense during incidents. keyIdea.title: Guardrail vs grant
keyIdea.text: SCPs limit the maximum permissions at the account/OU level. IAM policies grant specific permissions inside those limits.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › SCPs vs IAM Policies
Service Control Policies
Apply at organization or OU scope and limit the maximum permissions available in member accounts.
Use case:
Deny s3:DeleteBucket in production OU to protect audit data.
IAM Policies
Attach to identities or resources to grant or deny actions within the SCP boundary.
Use case:
Grant ec2:RebootInstances for a diagnostic role in the production account.
Design guidance
  • Use SCPs as conservative guardrails for sensitive OUs.
  • Keep IAM policies focused and minimal inside SCP constraints.
  • Test SCP effects before applying to production to avoid accidental service denial.

screens.title: Common Security Mistakes During Incident Response
screens.subtitle: Recognize and mitigate common pitfalls that increase risk during incidents

narration.text: During incidents pressure drives mistakes. Recognize the common pitfalls so you can design controls to prevent them. First, over-privileged roles given ‘just in case’ widen attack surface — avoid AdministratorAccess and prepare narrowly scoped roles by task. Second, lack of MFA for elevated roles removes the critical second factor that can block unauthorized assume-role attempts. Third, long-lived credentials permit ongoing access if exposed; prefer STS temporary credentials issued at assume time. Fourth, no audit trail makes forensic analysis impossible, so ensure CloudTrail records assume-role and privileged A P I calls. Fifth, neglecting SCPs leaves destructive actions possible across accounts; use SCPs to deny actions like deleting logs. Mitigations include permission reviews, break-glass procedures with approvals and short sessions, enforced MFA in trust policies, STS usage, and org-level SCPs. A helpful exercise is a post-incident dry run: assume roles with and without MFA, attempt prohibited actions and confirm SCP enforcement, and review CloudTrail to verify logs and alerts. In practical terms, recognize and mitigate common pitfalls that increase risk during incidents. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Designing a Break-Glass Emergency Access Procedure
screens.subtitle: Controlled, auditable emergency access for extreme situations

narration.text: A break-glass procedure is an emergency access path used only when normal channels cannot resolve an outage. Because this role is highly privileged, design it with the strictest controls: require multi-party approval, short time-limited sessions, and extensive logging and alerts. Operationally, store the procedure in runbooks that document who can authorize, how to request access, and how to record evidence of its use. Technical controls include enabling MFA, requiring an approval workflow that triggers temporary STS credentials, and integrating alerts to notify security and compliance teams when the role is assumed. Regular audits and simulated drills help ensure the break-glass path remains secure and functional. A misconception is that break-glass removes the need for narrow roles; it does not. Use break-glass only in true emergencies and keep narrow scoped roles for routine incident work. After any break-glass use, perform a full post-incident review to validate actions taken and to return the environment to normal operating posture. Designing a Break-Glass Emergency Access Procedure means emergency roles are tightly controlled, time-limited, approved, and auditable; they are not a substitute for narrow daily responder roles.. In practical terms, controlled, auditable emergency access for extreme situations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Hands-on: Configure Cross-Account Role with MFA Enforcement
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step configuration and CLI test to validate MFA-based assume-role

narration.text: This hands-on exercise walks you through creating a CrossAccountIncidentResponder role in a target account and configuring your primary account to assume it with MFA. First, in the primary account ensure your IAM user has MFA and the policy that allows sts:AssumeRole for the target role. Second, in the target account create the CrossAccountIncidentResponder role and attach a trust policy that allows the primary account's root or a specific role to assume it, requiring aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent. Attach a permissions policy scoped to the tasks a responder will perform, for example read-only diagnostics and SSM automation actions. Third, configure a CLI profile that references role_arn, source_profile, and mfa_serial so the CLI will prompt for your MFA code when assuming the role. Finally, test by running an AWS CLI describe command using the cross-account profile. If you omit the MFA code the assume call should fail, proving enforcement. After validation, review CloudTrail to confirm the assume-role event and the issued temporary credentials. This exercise reinforces secure assume-role practices and verifies that guardrails work as intended. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Remember these core definitions and why they matter

narration.text: Let's lock in the essential concepts. First, the Principle of Least Privilege: always give responders only the permissions needed for their task to reduce blast radius. Second, IAM Roles: roles are identities with permissions that can be assumed by trusted entities; prefer roles for incident response rather than sharing user keys. Third, Cross-Account Access: use cross-account roles and trust policies to let a central security team access resources in other accounts without granting permanent rights. These three ideas work together: narrow roles scoped per task, assumed by trusted identities from a central account, enforce least privilege while maintaining operational reach. As you design systems, ask whether a responder's access can be narrowed further, whether MFA is enforced at assume time, and whether the action could be blocked by an SCP. If the answer is no, iterate the design until it meets these checks.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Least privilege, IAM roles, and cross-account trust form the foundation of secure incident access.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts — Part 1
Principle of Least Privilege
Grant only needed permissions to minimize exploitation if credentials are compromised.
IAM Roles
Identities with attachable policies that can be assumed by trusted principals.
Cross-Account Access
Allow a principal in one account to assume a role in another using trust policies and conditions.
Summary takeaway

Combine narrow roles, MFA enforcement, and cross-account trust to enable secure, auditable incident response.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Additional definitions to keep in mind

narration.text: Finish with the remaining concepts that matter in incident response. Multi-Factor Authentication is the additional authentication capability that prevents role assumption without the second factor; require it in trust policies for elevated roles. AWS Organizations Service Control Policies define organization-level guardrails to prevent destructive actions even if an IAM policy would otherwise allow them. AWS Security Token Service issues temporary credentials that expire; use STS for assume-role flows to avoid long-lived egress keys. Keep these concepts in mind as a checklist when you design incident access: require MFA, use STS for temporary sessions, and apply SCPs to protect logs and critical infrastructure. These layered controls make it much harder for an attacker to misuse responder privileges and ensure forensic trails remain intact for post-incident analysis. In practical terms, additional definitions to keep in mind. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Multi-Factor Authentication
Require an additional factor for assume-role to protect elevated access.
Service Control Policies (SCPs)
Organization-level policies that apply preventive restrictions to all principals in scoped accounts.
AWS Security Token Service (STS)
Issues temporary credentials for assumed roles, limiting exposure from compromised keys.
Summary takeaway

Combine MFA, STS, and SCPs for layered protection and forensic integrity during incident response.
